lesson.title: The Envelope for the Wire: What a Frame Actually Carries
lesson.summary: A frame is the unit of data used at the link layer, wrapping a message with addressing and error-checking information so that devices sharing one physical link know where a message starts, who it is for, and whether it arrived intact.
lesson.body:
A raw electrical signal or radio wave flowing across a network cable or through the air has no inherent boundaries. It is just a continuous stream of ones and zeros until something imposes structure on it, and that is exactly what a frame does. A frame is the unit of data used at the link layer, the layer responsible for one physical hop between two devices sharing the same local link, and its name literally describes its job: it frames a chunk of data with a header and trailer that mark where the message begins, who it is addressed to, and where it ends.

The Ethernet frame format, standardized by IEEE 802.3, shows exactly what this structure looks like in bytes. A preamble and start frame delimiter, together 8 bytes, come first and exist purely to let the receiving hardware synchronize its clock to the sender's timing before any real content arrives. Next comes a 6-byte destination MAC address and a 6-byte source MAC address, identifying which network card sent the frame and which one it is meant for. A 2-byte EtherType field follows, typically identifying what kind of data the frame is carrying, such as an IPv4 packet. Then comes the actual payload, which can range from 46 to 1,500 bytes. Finally, a 4-byte Frame Check Sequence, a CRC-32 checksum, closes out the frame, giving the receiver a way to detect whether any bits were corrupted in transit. Adding this up, a standard Ethernet frame runs from a minimum of 64 bytes to a maximum of 1,518 bytes, not counting the preamble.

Each piece of that structure exists to solve a specific problem. The addressing fields let a switch connected to many devices on a shared local segment figure out which port to forward an incoming frame out of, rather than blasting every frame to every device. The checksum lets the receiving device detect, though not correct, damage caused by electrical noise or interference on the wire, and simply discard a frame that got corrupted rather than pass bad data further up the stack. The preamble solves a purely physical problem, giving both ends of the link time to agree on timing before the meaningful bits start.

This exact byte layout only works because it is defined precisely, in a standard, down to the individual byte, exactly the kind of precision the earlier chapters on protocols and standards described as essential. Every network card manufacturer builds hardware that reads and writes this identical format specified by IEEE 802.3, which is why a network card made by one company can exchange frames with a switch made by an entirely different one without either company needing to coordinate directly, echoing the shipping-container example from the Standard chapter almost exactly.

A frame's scope is deliberately narrow: it only makes sense across a single physical link between two directly connected devices, or between a device and a switch on the same local network. When data needs to travel further, across multiple networks toward a distant destination, something has to be carried inside a fresh frame at every hop along the way. That something is a packet, which is exactly where the next chapter picks up.
